L6.2 - Overview of Shell Scripts

Bash Shell Scripting

Shell scripting is the process of writing a sequence of shell commands into a file so that the commands can be executed automatically.

Instead of typing:

mkdir backup
cp file.txt backup/
echo "Backup completed"

every time, we can put these commands into a script:

#!/bin/bash

mkdir backup
cp file.txt backup/
echo "Backup completed"

and execute the script.

The main idea is:

Commands
   ↓
Script file
   ↓
Shell interprets the commands
   ↓
Task is automated

1. What Is a Script?

A script is a text file containing commands that a shell can execute.

For example:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Hello"
date
pwd
ls

Save it as:

hello.sh

Then execute it.

A shell script can contain:

  • commands
  • variables
  • input
  • arguments
  • conditions
  • loops
  • functions
  • command substitution
  • file operations

This allows us to build useful automation programs using the shell.

2. Types of Scripts

There are several ways to classify scripts.

2.1 Shell Scripts

A shell script is interpreted by a shell such as:

bash
sh
zsh

Example:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Hello from Bash"

2.2 Executed Scripts

A script can be executed as a separate process.

Example:

./script.sh

The shell starts a process to interpret the script.

2.3 Sourced Scripts

A script can also be sourced into the current shell:

source script.sh

or:

. script.sh

The commands execute inside the current shell environment.

This distinction is extremely important.

3. Shebang

A shebang is the first line of an executable script that specifies which interpreter should run it.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

The first two characters are:

#!

followed by the interpreter path.

For Bash:

#!/bin/bash

Another common form is:

#!/usr/bin/env bash

This asks env to locate bash using the environment’s PATH.

4. Why Do We Need a Shebang?

Suppose a script contains:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Hello"

When you execute:

./script.sh

the operating system uses the interpreter specified by the shebang.

Conceptually:

./script.sh
     ↓
#!/bin/bash
     ↓
/bin/bash
     ↓
execute script

Without a shebang, the behavior depends on how the script is invoked.

For example:

bash script.sh

explicitly tells Bash to interpret it, so the shebang is not required for that invocation.

5. Making a Script Executable

Create:

nano hello.sh

Put:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Hello World"

Save it.

Initially, the file may not have execute permission.

Check:

ls -l hello.sh

Give it execute permission:

chmod +x hello.sh

Then:

./hello.sh

Output:

Hello World

6. Sourcing vs Executing

This is one of the most important shell scripting concepts.

There are two different ways to run a script.

Execute

./script.sh

or:

bash script.sh

Source

source script.sh

or:

. script.sh

The major difference is the shell environment in which the commands execute.

7. Executing a Script

Suppose script.sh contains:

#!/bin/bash

name="Shubham"
echo "$name"

Run:

./script.sh

The script runs in a separate shell process.

After it finishes:

echo "$name"

in your original shell will generally produce nothing because the variable was created in the script’s shell.

Mental model:

Parent shell
     │
     └── starts script shell
              │
              ├── name="Shubham"
              └── exits

The variable disappears with that child shell.

8. Sourcing a Script

Suppose the same script contains:

name="Shubham"

Run:

source script.sh

Now:

echo "$name"

will output:

Shubham

Why?

Because the script was executed inside the current shell.

Mental model:

Current shell
     │
     ├── name="Shubham"
     ├── echo
     └── continues

No separate shell is created just to interpret the sourced script.

9. Practical Difference

Create:

nano variables.sh

Contents:

#!/bin/bash

course="Linux"

Execute:

./variables.sh
echo "$course"

The variable is not normally available in the parent shell.

Now source:

source variables.sh
echo "$course"

Output:

Linux

Remember

./script.sh
    ↓
separate execution environment

source script.sh
    ↓
current shell environment

Sourcing is commonly used for:

  • shell configuration
  • environment variables
  • functions
  • aliases
  • activation scripts

For example:

source ~/.bashrc

10. Script Location

When you execute:

./script.sh

the ./ means:

Look for script.sh in the current directory.

For example:

pwd

might show:

/home/user/scripts

Then:

./backup.sh

means:

/home/user/scripts/backup.sh

11. Running a Script from Another Directory

Suppose:

/home/user/scripts/backup.sh

You are currently in:

/home/user

You can execute:

./scripts/backup.sh

or:

/home/user/scripts/backup.sh

if it is executable.

You can also invoke it through Bash:

bash /home/user/scripts/backup.sh

12. Bash Environment

Every running shell has an environment containing variables and other shell state.

Common variables include:

$USER
$HOME
$PATH
$PWD
$HOSTNAME

Example:

echo "$USER"

echo "$HOME"

echo "$PATH"

echo "$PWD"

13. Environment Variables vs Shell Variables

A shell variable:

name="Shubham"

exists in the current shell.

To export it:

export name

Now child processes can inherit it.

Example:

export course="Linux"
bash -c 'echo "$course"'

Output:

Linux

The child shell receives a copy of the exported variable.

14. echo

echo prints text or variable values.

Basic example:

echo "hello world"

Output:

hello world

Multiple arguments:

echo Hello World

Output:

Hello World

Another example:

echo "Linux" "Bash" "Scripting"

Output:

Linux Bash Scripting

15. Quotes with echo

Single Quotes

name="Shubham"

echo '$name'

Output:

$name

Single quotes prevent variable expansion.

Double Quotes

name="Shubham"

echo "$name"

Output:

Shubham

Double quotes allow variable expansion.

No Quotes

echo $name

This may work for simple values, but quoting variables is generally safer:

echo "$name"

16. printf

printf is a more predictable and flexible way to produce formatted output.

Example:

printf "Hello World\n"

Output:

Hello World

The \n means newline.

Variables:

name="Shubham"

printf "Hello, %s\n" "$name"

Output:

Hello, Shubham

Here:

%s

means:

format the argument as a string.

17. printf vs echo

For simple output:

echo "Hello"

is convenient.

For reliable formatting:

printf "Hello, %s\n" "$name"

is generally preferred in scripts.

Example:

printf "Name: %s\nAge: %d\n" "Shubham" 27

Output:

Name: Shubham
Age: 27

18. Reading Input with read

The read command reads input from the user.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Enter your name:"
read name

echo "Hello $name"

Run:

./script.sh

Interaction:

Enter your name:
Shubham
Hello Shubham

The basic model is:

User types input
       ↓
      read
       ↓
variable receives value

19. read -p

Instead of using a separate echo:

read -p "Enter your name: " name

Example:

#!/bin/bash

read -p "Enter your name: " name
printf "Hello, %s\n" "$name"

20. Reading Multiple Values

read -p "Enter your first and last name: " first last

If the user enters:

Shubham Vithalkar

then:

first = Shubham
last  = Vithalkar

The splitting behavior is affected by IFS.

21. Script Arguments

A script can receive values from the command line.

Suppose:

#!/bin/bash

echo "$0"
echo "$1"
echo "$2"

Run:

./script.sh hello world

Possible output:

./script.sh
hello
world

Here:

$0 → script name
$1 → first argument
$2 → second argument

22. Positional Parameters

Important positional parameters:

$0
$1
$2
$3
...
$9

Example:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Script: $0"
echo "First: $1"
echo "Second: $2"

Run:

./script.sh Linux Bash

Output:

Script: ./script.sh
First: Linux
Second: Bash

23. $#

$# contains the number of positional arguments.

Script:

#!/bin/bash

echo "Number of arguments: $#"

Run:

./script.sh one two three

Output:

Number of arguments: 3

24. $@

$@ represents all positional arguments.

Example:

#!/bin/bash

echo "$@"

Run:

./script.sh one two three

Output:

one two three

In scripts, prefer:

"$@"

when you want to preserve each argument as a separate word.

25. $*

$* also represents positional arguments, but its behavior differs from "$@" when quoted.

The important distinction is:

"$@"

expands positional parameters as separate words.

"$*"

typically joins them into a single word using the first character of IFS.

For example, with:

one
two words
three

"$@" preserves these as three separate arguments.

This makes "$@" the usual choice when forwarding arguments:

some_command "$@"

26. $@ vs $*

Remember:

"$@"
 ↓
each argument remains separate

"$*"
 ↓
arguments are combined into one word

This distinction becomes important when arguments contain spaces.

27. Command Substitution

Command substitution allows us to capture the output of a command and use it as a value.

Modern syntax:

$(command)

Example:

today=$(date)
echo "$today"

The date command executes first.

Its output is stored in:

today

Then:

echo "$today"

prints it.

28. Another Command Substitution Example

current_dir=$(pwd)

echo "You are in: $current_dir"

Possible output:

You are in: /home/user/project

Another example:

files=$(ls)

echo "$files"

Mental model

command
   ↓
output
   ↓
$(...)
   ↓
variable

29. Command Substitution vs Quotes

Use:

today=$(date)

not the old-style:

today=`date`

Backticks work, but $(...) is preferred because it is easier to read and nest.

For example:

result=$(dirname "$(pwd)")

30. for Loop

A for loop repeats commands for multiple values.

Basic syntax:

for item in one two three
do
    echo "$item"
done

Output:

one
two
three

The loop works like:

item = one
  ↓
execute body

item = two
  ↓
execute body

item = three
  ↓
execute body

31. for Loop with Files

Example:

for file in *.txt
do
    echo "$file"
done

This processes each matching .txt pathname.

Example output:

a.txt
b.txt
notes.txt

Be careful when filenames contain spaces; quote the variable:

echo "$file"

32. C-Style for Loop

Bash also supports:

for ((i=1; i<=5; i++))
do
    echo "$i"
done

Output:

1
2
3
4
5

This is useful when you need numeric iteration.

33. IFS — Internal Field Separator

IFS stands for:

Internal Field Separator

It controls how Bash performs word splitting in contexts where word splitting occurs.

The default value generally contains:

space
tab
newline

You can inspect it with:

printf '%q\n' "$IFS"

34. Why Is IFS Important?

Suppose:

text="Linux Bash Shell"

and:

for word in $text
do
    echo "$word"
done

Because the default IFS contains spaces, Bash splits the value into words:

Linux
Bash
Shell

Conceptually:

"Linux Bash Shell"
       ↓
     IFS
       ↓
Linux | Bash | Shell

35. Changing IFS

You can temporarily set IFS.

For example:

IFS=:

Now colon can be used as a field separator.

This is useful when processing colon-separated data such as:

name:age:city

Example:

IFS=: read name age city <<< "Shubham:27:Bilaspur"

echo "$name"
echo "$age"
echo "$city"

Output:

Shubham
27
Bilaspur

36. case Statement

Bash’s case statement is similar to a switch statement in many programming languages.

Basic syntax:

case "$value" in
    pattern1)
        commands
        ;;
    pattern2)
        commands
        ;;
    *)
        default commands
        ;;
esac

The statement ends with:

esac

which is case spelled backwards.

37. case Example

read -p "Enter a number: " number

case "$number" in
    1)
        echo "One"
        ;;
    2)
        echo "Two"
        ;;
    3)
        echo "Three"
        ;;
    *)
        echo "Something else"
        ;;
esac

If the user enters:

2

output:

Two

38. case with Patterns

case patterns use shell pattern matching.

Example:

case "$1" in
    *.txt)
        echo "Text file"
        ;;
    *.jpg|*.png)
        echo "Image file"
        ;;
    *)
        echo "Unknown file type"
        ;;
esac

Run:

./check.sh photo.jpg

Output:

Image file

39. if Statement

The if statement performs conditional execution.

Basic syntax:

if condition
then
    commands
fi

The statement ends with:

fi

which is if backwards.

40. Basic if Example

if [ "$1" = "hello" ]
then
    echo "You said hello"
fi

Run:

./script.sh hello

Output:

You said hello

41. if, elif, else

Full structure:

if condition
then
    commands
elif another_condition
then
    commands
else
    commands
fi

Example:

read -p "Enter your age: " age

if [ "$age" -ge 18 ]
then
    echo "Adult"
else
    echo "Minor"
fi

42. Conditions

Bash conditions can test:

  • strings
  • numbers
  • files
  • command exit status
  • logical combinations

For example:

if [ "$name" = "Shubham" ]
then
    echo "Name matched"
fi

43. String Comparisons

Common string operators:

=       equal
!=      not equal
-z      string is empty
-n      string is not empty

Example:

name="Shubham"

if [ "$name" = "Shubham" ]
then
    echo "Matched"
fi

Not equal:

if [ "$name" != "Rahul" ]
then
    echo "Different"
fi

Empty:

if [ -z "$name" ]
then
    echo "Empty"
fi

Non-empty:

if [ -n "$name" ]
then
    echo "Not empty"
fi

44. Numeric Comparisons

For integer comparisons, use:

-eq    equal
-ne    not equal
-lt    less than
-le    less than or equal
-gt    greater than
-ge    greater than or equal

Example:

age=27

if [ "$age" -ge 18 ]
then
    echo "Adult"
fi

Important

Do not confuse:

[ "$a" = "$b" ]

with:

[ "$a" -eq "$b" ]

The first is string comparison.

The second is integer comparison.

45. Modern [[ ... ]]

Bash also provides:

[[ ... ]]

Example:

if [[ "$name" == "Shubham" ]]
then
    echo "Matched"
fi

For Bash scripts, [[ ... ]] is often safer and more expressive than the traditional [ ... ].

Example:

if [[ "$name" == S* ]]
then
    echo "Starts with S"
fi

Here S* is a shell pattern.

46. File Comparisons

Bash provides file-test operators.

Common ones:

-e file    exists
-f file    regular file
-d file    directory
-r file    readable
-w file    writable
-x file    executable
-s file    exists and has non-zero size

Example:

if [ -f "data.txt" ]
then
    echo "Regular file exists"
fi

47. Directory Test

if [ -d "backup" ]
then
    echo "Backup directory exists"
fi

48. Executable Test

if [ -x "script.sh" ]
then
    echo "Script is executable"
fi

49. File Size Test

if [ -s "data.txt" ]
then
    echo "File is not empty"
fi

50. File Comparison by Modification Time

Bash also provides operators such as:

-nt    newer than
-ot    older than

Example:

if [ "new.txt" -nt "old.txt" ]
then
    echo "new.txt is newer"
fi

Another:

if [ "old.txt" -ot "new.txt" ]
then
    echo "old.txt is older"
fi

51. Combining Conditions

Logical AND:

if [[ "$age" -ge 18 && "$age" -le 60 ]]
then
    echo "Working-age range"
fi

Logical OR:

if [[ "$name" == "Shubham" || "$name" == "Rahul" ]]
then
    echo "Known name"
fi

Negation:

if [[ ! -f "data.txt" ]]
then
    echo "File does not exist"
fi

52. Command Exit Status in Conditions

Linux commands return an exit status.

Generally:

0       success
nonzero failure/other condition

Example:

if grep -q "ERROR" server.log
then
    echo "ERROR found"
else
    echo "No ERROR found"
fi

The if statement checks the exit status of grep.

This is one of the most important Bash concepts:

command
   ↓
exit status
   ↓
if
   ↓
decision

53. while Loop

A while loop repeatedly executes commands while its condition succeeds.

Basic syntax:

while condition
do
    commands
done

Example:

count=1

while [ "$count" -le 5 ]
do
    echo "$count"
    count=$((count + 1))
done

Output:

1
2
3
4
5

54. How the while Loop Works

Check condition
      ↓
  condition true?
    /       \
  yes        no
   ↓          ↓
execute      stop
body
   ↓
check again

For:

while [ "$count" -le 5 ]

the loop continues while count is less than or equal to 5.

55. Reading a File with while

A common Bash pattern is:

while IFS= read -r line
do
    echo "$line"
done < input.txt

This reads the file line by line.

Important:

IFS=

prevents leading/trailing whitespace from being stripped by read.

-r

prevents backslashes from being interpreted as escape characters.

This is a robust pattern for reading text files line by line.

56. Functions

A function is a reusable group of commands.

Instead of writing:

echo "Starting"
date
echo "Finished"

multiple times, put the logic into a function.

Basic syntax:

function_name() {
    commands
}

Example:

hello() {
    echo "Hello World"
}

Call it:

hello

Output:

Hello World

57. Function Arguments

Functions can receive arguments using positional parameters.

Example:

greet() {
    echo "Hello, $1"
}

greet "Shubham"

Output:

Hello, Shubham

Inside the function:

$1

means the first argument passed to the function.

58. Multiple Function Arguments

add() {
    echo $(( $1 + $2 ))
}

add 10 20

Output:

30

The function receives:

$1 = 10
$2 = 20

59. Function Return Status

A Bash function can return an exit status.

Example:

check_file() {
    if [ -f "$1" ]
    then
        return 0
    else
        return 1
    fi
}

Use it:

if check_file "data.txt"
then
    echo "File exists"
else
    echo "File does not exist"
fi

Remember:

return 0
    ↓
success

return non-zero
    ↓
failure/false condition

60. Function Output

Functions can also produce output with echo or printf.

Example:

get_date() {
    date
}

result=$(get_date)

echo "$result"

This combines:

function
   ↓
command output
   ↓
command substitution

61. Complete Example

Here is a small Bash script combining several concepts:

#!/bin/bash

read -p "Enter your name: " name

if [[ -z "$name" ]]
then
    echo "Name cannot be empty"
    exit 1
fi

greet() {
    printf "Hello, %s!\n" "$1"
}

today=$(date "+%Y-%m-%d")

greet "$name"

echo "Today is: $today"

for item in Linux Bash Scripting
do
    echo "Learning: $item"
done

Possible execution:

Enter your name: Shubham
Hello, Shubham!
Today is: 2026-09-08
Learning: Linux
Learning: Bash
Learning: Scripting

This one script demonstrates:

shebang
read
if
[[ ]]
function
printf
command substitution
for loop
variables
arguments

62. Script Arguments + Conditions

A practical script can use command-line arguments:

#!/bin/bash

if [ "$#" -lt 1 ]
then
    echo "Usage: $0 filename"
    exit 1
fi

if [ -f "$1" ]
then
    echo "$1 is a regular file"
else
    echo "$1 is not a regular file"
fi

Run:

./check.sh data.txt

Possible output:

data.txt is a regular file

Run without arguments:

./check.sh

Output:

Usage: ./check.sh filename

63. Practical Script: File Backup

#!/bin/bash

if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]
then
    echo "Usage: $0 directory"
    exit 1
fi

if [ ! -d "$1" ]
then
    echo "Directory does not exist"
    exit 1
fi

backup="backup-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).tar.gz"

tar -czf "$backup" "$1"

echo "Backup created: $backup"

Run:

./backup.sh logfiles

The script:

$#
 ↓
checks number of arguments

$1
 ↓
gets directory

-d
 ↓
checks directory

$(date ...)
 ↓
generates timestamp

tar
 ↓
creates backup

64. Important Bash Syntax to Remember

Variable

name="Shubham"

Use variable

echo "$name"

Command substitution

result=$(command)

Read input

read name

Script argument

$1

Number of arguments

$#

All arguments

"$@"

If

if condition
then
    commands
fi

Case

case "$x" in
    pattern)
        commands
        ;;
esac

For

for x in a b c
do
    commands
done

While

while condition
do
    commands
done

Function

name() {
    commands
}

65. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Spaces around variable assignment

Wrong:

name = "Shubham"

Correct:

name="Shubham"

Mistake 2: Forgetting $

Wrong:

echo "name"

This prints:

name

Correct:

echo "$name"

Mistake 3: Not quoting variables

Prefer:

echo "$name"

instead of:

echo $name

Especially important for filenames and values containing spaces.

Mistake 4: Confusing $# and $@

$#
 ↓
number of arguments

$@
 ↓
arguments themselves

Mistake 5: Using $* when you need separate arguments

When forwarding arguments, prefer:

command "$@"

rather than:

command "$*"

Mistake 6: Forgetting fi

Wrong:

if [ "$x" = "yes" ]
then
    echo "Yes"

Correct:

if [ "$x" = "yes" ]
then
    echo "Yes"
fi

Mistake 7: Forgetting esac

Correct:

case "$x" in
    yes)
        echo "Yes"
        ;;
    no)
        echo "No"
        ;;
esac

Mistake 8: Infinite while loop

This can run forever:

count=1

while [ "$count" -le 5 ]
do
    echo "$count"
done

count never changes.

Correct:

count=1

while [ "$count" -le 5 ]
do
    echo "$count"
    count=$((count + 1))
done

66. Exam Perspective

You should be able to explain the difference between:

./script.sh

and:

source script.sh

You should know:

$0   script name
$1   first argument
$2   second argument
$#   argument count
$@   all arguments
$*   all arguments, different quoting behavior

You should know:

if    → fi
case  → esac
for   → done
while → done

You should know:

$(command)

means command substitution.

You should know:

IFS

controls word splitting in relevant shell operations.

You should know the difference between:

=      string comparison
-eq    integer comparison
-f     regular file
-d     directory
-e     exists
-r     readable
-w     writable
-x     executable

You should know:

return 0

means successful function status, while a non-zero status generally indicates failure or another condition.

67. Practice Questions

Q1

Create a Bash script that prints:

Hello World

Solution

#!/bin/bash

echo "Hello World"

Q2

Write a script that accepts a name as its first argument and prints:

Hello, <name>

Solution

#!/bin/bash

echo "Hello, $1"

Run:

./hello.sh Shubham

Q3

Write a script that prints the number of arguments.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

echo "Arguments: $#"

Q4

Write a script that prints every argument separately.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

for arg in "$@"
do
    echo "$arg"
done

Q5

Write a script that asks the user for their name using read.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

read -p "Enter your name: " name
echo "Hello, $name"

Q6

Write a script that stores the output of date in a variable.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

today=$(date)

echo "$today"

Q7

Write a script that checks whether the first argument is a regular file.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

if [ -f "$1" ]
then
    echo "Regular file"
else
    echo "Not a regular file"
fi

Q8

Write a script that checks whether the first argument is a directory.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

if [ -d "$1" ]
then
    echo "Directory"
else
    echo "Not a directory"
fi

Q9

Write a for loop that prints numbers from 1 to 5.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

for ((i=1; i<=5; i++))
do
    echo "$i"
done

Q10

Write a while loop that prints numbers from 1 to 5.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

i=1

while [ "$i" -le 5 ]
do
    echo "$i"
    i=$((i + 1))
done

Q11

Write a case statement that prints:

start → Starting
stop  → Stopping
*     → Unknown command

Solution

#!/bin/bash

case "$1" in
    start)
        echo "Starting"
        ;;
    stop)
        echo "Stopping"
        ;;
    *)
        echo "Unknown command"
        ;;
esac

Q12

Write a function called greet that accepts a name.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

greet() {
    echo "Hello, $1"
}

greet "Shubham"

Q13 — Exam Level

Write a script that:

  1. Requires exactly one argument.
  2. Checks whether it is a regular file.
  3. Prints its size using du -h.
  4. Prints an error if the argument is not a file.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]
then
    echo "Usage: $0 filename"
    exit 1
fi

if [ -f "$1" ]
then
    du -h "$1"
else
    echo "Not a regular file"
    exit 1
fi

Q14 — Exam Level

Write a script that accepts any number of filenames and prints only the files that exist.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

for file in "$@"
do
    if [ -e "$file" ]
    then
        echo "$file"
    fi
done

Q15 — Exam Level

Write a script that asks for a directory and then prints all .log files inside it.

Solution

#!/bin/bash

read -p "Enter directory: " dir

if [ ! -d "$dir" ]
then
    echo "Directory does not exist"
    exit 1
fi

for file in "$dir"/*.log
do
    if [ -f "$file" ]
    then
        echo "$file"
    fi
done

68. Final Mental Model

BASH SCRIPT
│
├── Shebang
│     └── #!/bin/bash
│
├── Input
│     ├── read
│     └── arguments: $1, $2, ...
│
├── Variables
│     ├── $USER
│     ├── $HOME
│     └── custom variables
│
├── Output
│     ├── echo
│     └── printf
│
├── Command substitution
│     └── $(command)
│
├── Decisions
│     ├── if
│     └── case
│
├── Loops
│     ├── for
│     └── while
│
├── Data splitting
│     └── IFS
│
└── Reusable logic
      └── functions

Core Bash Script Pattern

#!/bin/bash

# Input
read -p "Enter something: " value

# Decision
if [[ -n "$value" ]]
then
    echo "You entered: $value"
else
    echo "Nothing entered"
fi

# Loop
for item in one two three
do
    echo "$item"
done

# Function
greet() {
    echo "Hello, $1"
}

greet "$value"

The key progression to remember is:

Commands
   ↓
Variables
   ↓
Input / Arguments
   ↓
Command Substitution
   ↓
Conditions
   ↓
Loops
   ↓
Functions
   ↓
Complete Automation Scripts
